'''Simeon James Rice''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|s|ɪ|m|i|ən}} {{respell|SIM|ee|ən}}; born February 24, 1974) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[defensive end]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Illinois Fighting Illini football|Illinois Fighting Illini]], and is the all-time sack leader in the [[Big Ten|Big Ten Conference]].<ref>{{cite web |title=www.cfbhall.com |url=https://www.cfbhall.com/news-and-happenings/news/2026-college-football-hall-of-fame-ballot-officially-announced/}}</ref> Rice was selected by the [[Arizona Cardinals]] third overall in the [[1996 NFL draft]].

In his 12-year NFL career, Rice recorded 122 [[quarterback sack|sacks]], forced 25 [[fumble]]s, recovered 8, and [[interception|intercepted]] 5 passes. His official sack count ranks 23rd all-time in the NFL.<ref>{{Cite web |title=NFL Sacks Career Leaders (Since 1960) |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/leaders/sacks_career.htm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161126090410/http://www.pro-football-reference.com/leaders/sacks_career.htm |archive-date=November 26, 2016 |access-date=November 18, 2022 |website=[[Pro-Football-Reference.com]]}}</ref> In his first eight out of 10 seasons in the NFL, Rice recorded at least 10 sacks and in three of those seasons he recorded at least 15 sacks. He earned three [[Pro Bowl]] selections and earned a [[Super Bowl ring]] with the [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]] in [[Super Bowl XXXVII]], beating the [[Oakland Raiders]]. He has also played for the [[Denver Broncos]], [[Indianapolis Colts]], and [[Hartford Colonials|New York Sentinels]].

'''Brian LaVell''' "'''Skip'''" '''Hicks''' (born October 13, 1974) is an American former professional [[Gridiron football|football]] player who was a [[running back]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He was selected in the third round of the 1998 NFL Draft.<ref>{{Cite web |title=1998 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1998/draft.htm |access-date=2023-03-29 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> In his four seasons, Hicks played for the [[Washington Redskins]]<ref>{{cite news|url=https://news.google.ca/newspapers?id=fgMzAAAAIBAJ&sjid=2wgGAAAAIBAJ&pg=6226,5794369&dq=skip-hicks&hl=en|title=Redskins Starters Flex Muscles Against Browns|date=19 August 2000|work=[[Free-Lance Star]]|access-date=30 August 2010}}</ref> and the [[Tennessee Titans]].<ref>{{Cite news |date=14 December 2001 |title=Mcnair Hicks Pace Tennessee |url=https://news.google.ca/newspapers?id=_vYrAAAAIBAJ&sjid=Fm0FAAAAIBAJ&pg=4352,7336111&dq=skip-hicks+titans&hl=en |access-date=30 August 2010 |work=[[Kentucky New Era]]|via=[[Google News]]}}</ref>  He played [[college football]] for the [[UCLA Bruins football|UCLA Bruins]] and still holds school records for touchdowns in a season, with 26 in 1997, and career touchdowns, with 55 (1993–94, 96–97).  He graduated from [[Burkburnett High School]] in [[Burkburnett, Texas]] in 1993.

Hicks also played for the [[Toronto Argonauts]] of the [[Canadian Football League]] in [[2004 CFL season|2004]], appearing in two games.  The Argonauts went on to win the [[92nd Grey Cup]] that year, but Hicks was not dressed for that game.

'''Sloan Thomas''' (born December 22, 1981) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] [[wide receiver]] from the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He went to [[Klein High School]] in [[Klein, Texas]]. He played in 46 games for the [[University of Texas]], [[Starting lineup|starting]] 20 contests. He caught 88 passes (ranked 10th on the school's career-record list) for 1,362 yards and 12 touchdowns (tied for seventh on the school record list). He was selected by the [[Houston Texans]] in the seventh round of the [[2004 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2004/draft.htm |title=2004 NFL Draft Listing |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en |access-date=2023-05-06}}</ref> On August 31, 2006, Thomas was claimed off of waivers by the [[New York Jets]]. He was cut during the next training camp. He also spent time with the [[Seattle Seahawks]] in 2006.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://profootballarchives.com/transactions/t/thom14850.html | title=Sloan Thomas | publisher=profootballarchives.com | accessdate=May 14, 2024}}</ref>

'''Alonzo''' "'''Skip'''" '''Thomas III''' (February 7, 1950 – July 24, 2011), nicknamed "'''Dr. Death'''", was an American professional [[American football|football]] player. A [[cornerback]], Thomas played college football at [[Arizona Western College|Arizona Western Junior College]] before transferring to the [[USC Trojans football|University of Southern California]]. After college, he spent six seasons with the [[Oakland Raiders]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL) before retiring from football. 

Thomas was a part of the Raiders' [[Super Bowl XI]] winning team, and a notable figure in the "Soul Patrol" defensive secondary of the 1970s. Alongside cornerback [[Jack Tatum]] and safeties [[Willie Brown (American football)|Willie Brown]] and [[George Atkinson (safety)|George Atkinson]], the quartet were known for their physicality. Thomas' harsh style on the field is well documented, though he is remembered as the most subdued of the four.
